_comment: THE SOUL OF THE PRODUCT LIVES IN THIS FILE. Every value here is a starting point verified for syntax and determinism, not a tuned result -- expect a full pass at M1 against a real clip. That pass costs nothing, which is the entire reason this file exists separately from the code. Clamp ranges are enforced in scripts/tapedeck/look.mjs, not here, so this file stays readable and hand-editable.
_ordering: The filter order follows the physical signal path of a real camcorder: lens -> CCD -> camera DSP -> character generator -> tape encoder -> tape -> playback transport -> display. Do not reorder without reading the ordering rationale in docs/the-look.md; several reorderings are visually catastrophic in ways that are not obvious.

optics._comment: The lens, before any electronics. Bloom is halation on real scene light, so it must run before the grade -- reversed, you crush blacks and then add a glow that lifts them again.
optics._measured: vignette is far stronger than its angle suggests: PI/4.3 costs 45% of mean luma, PI/12 costs 20%, and even PI/20 costs 18%. It is applied twice (lens falloff here, canvas unifier at composite) so the losses compound. curveMaster carries the compensation -- do not raise either angle without re-measuring.

grade._comment: Camera DSP. curveMaster starting at 0/0.055 is the milky black floor -- consumer tape never reached true black, and crushing it to 0 is the fastest way to look like a modern camera with a filter on. Ending at 1/0.95 rolls the highlights off.

osd._comment: The character generator wrote this into the signal BEFORE the tape, so it degrades with the image but never picks up lens artifacts. dateText and timeText are literals computed in Node from the seed -- never %{localtime}, which reads the wall clock and destroys reproducibility. Colons in timeText are escaped at build time.

tape._comment: The tape encoder and the medium. chromaSmear is the star of the whole chain -- VHS chroma bandwidth was roughly a tenth of its luma bandwidth, which is why colour visibly runs off lips and brake lights. grainStrength is applied HERE, at 720x576, so it upscales into clumps larger than a pixel. Applied after the upscale it reads as a modern high-ISO sensor instead.

transport._comment: Playback mechanics, not recording. These displace the FINISHED tape image including its grain and its burnt-in date, which is why they run last. headSwitch is the constant noise band at the very bottom of frame -- the single most recognisable VHS tell, and it must never blink off. tears are the opposite: sparse, 1-2 across 15 seconds, noticeable once and then again just as you had forgotten.

composite._comment: The final vignette is applied to the WHOLE 1080x1920 canvas after the overlay, not to the tape image. That is what fuses tape and surround into one photographed object rather than two stacked layers, and it is the move that actually sells the framing.

audio._comment: The 'quiet' in 'warm, grainy, quiet'. Three synthesised layers, mono, band-limited, mixed low -- never a sample, because a synthesised bed's loudness is known a priori and therefore needs no normalisation pass. There is no loudnorm in the render and there must never be one: single-pass loudnorm applies dynamic, content-dependent gain, which pumps a steady hiss and makes the output a function of the analysis window instead of the seed. ebur128 belongs in the tests, asserting this target, never in the render reaching for it. The noise seed is `audioSeed` at the top of this file, next to the video seeds, because it is the same kind of thing.

hiss._comment: Mic self-noise plus preamp plus the tape's own floor. Pink rather than white because every one of those sources rolls off with frequency, and white noise reads as a digital fault rather than a room. The 8 kHz ceiling is the single strongest cue that dates the sound -- a camcorder's built-in electret had neither the diaphragm for real low end nor the bandwidth above it.

capstan._comment: The transport motor conducted through the chassis into the mic bolted to the same chassis. NOTE the tones are the motor HARMONICS, not its fundamental: a small DC capstan runs near 118 Hz, but the bus highpass sits at 190 Hz and a camcorder electret could not record 118 Hz in the first place, so voicing the fundamental would be specifying a tone that both the model of the mic and the graph itself throw away. 237 and 355 are its 2nd and 3rd harmonics and they survive to be heard. flutter is applied to the SUM, not per tone -- two independently wobbling partials beat against each other and read as an effect rather than as one machine. NOTE ALSO that a tone volume is not in the same units as hiss.amplitude: ffmpeg sine emits s16 at a fixed 4096/32768, so its intrinsic peak is 0.125 and volume 0.05 really means amplitude 0.00625.

bus._comment: Band-limit the sum a second time, apply the one fixed makeup gain, end in a real ceiling. The 190 Hz highpass is authentic -- a camcorder built-in mic had no low end -- which is why the capstan is voiced as harmonics above it rather than as its fundamental below it.

audio._measured: Calibration on ffmpeg 8.1.1, integrated LUFS of the bed straight out of the graph at masterGain 4.14: full bed -27.2, hiss alone -27.4, capstan alone -42.5. The hiss IS the bed; the capstan sits about 15 dB under it and is meant to be felt rather than identified. THREE TRAPS, ALL MEASURED. (1) Every amix carries normalize=0. ffmpeg defaults it to 1, which divides by the input count and silently scales away every level set here, and nothing else about the graph looks wrong. (2) alimiter carries level=disabled. Its "level" option defaults to auto, which scales output by 1/limit, so WITHOUT that flag "limit" is a gain control and lowering it to leave headroom makes the bed LOUDER. Measured: -29.6 with no limiter at all, -26.5 with limit=0.7 and auto level, -29.6 again with level=disabled. That is exactly 20*log10(1/0.7) = 3.1 dB of gain and zero samples limited. With level disabled, limit is a true ceiling, inert in normal use (true peak sits about 19 dB under it), and masterGain is the single control of loudness -- which is what the "level known a priori" design requires. (3) ffmpeg sine emits s16 at a fixed 4096/32768, so its intrinsic peak is 0.125: a tone volume of 0.03 is really amplitude 0.00375. Tone volumes are NOT in the same units as hiss.amplitude; do not read them against each other.

_notInBase: interlace is deliberately absent. On a progressive delivery target real field artifacts read as an encoding bug more often than as nostalgia, and the head-switch band already does about 80% of the 'this is tape' work for 5% of the risk. Add it only if M1 proves it earns its place.
